units.text: If an organism survives, has it obeyed the ‘law of the strongest’? Only if we retrospectively call every surviving organism ‘strong’. But then we have explained nothing. We have renamed the result.

In evolutionary theory, the relevant success is not reducible to muscular strength or individual survival. What matters is differential transmission of traits across generations in a concrete environment. An advantage in one environment can become a cost in another. Selection can favor resilience, fecundity, cooperation, conflict avoidance or exploitation of others, depending on relationships and conditions. It needs no conscious goal and guarantees no moral progress (Darwin, 1859/1872) .

This changes the meaning of a biological law. Part of the explanation is general: variation, heredity, reproductive differences. Another part is historical: which variations existed, in what order they appeared, which environment they encountered and what other traits accompanied them. The general principle does not replace a case’s causal history.

We can see the difference in an elementary genetic model. If two variants, A and a, have frequencies p and q, with p + q = 1, and the union of the two genetic contributions is independent and random, pair probabilities are p², 2pq and q². The calculation is the expansion of (p + q)². To interpret it as a Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, biological assumptions must also be specified, such as the absence of forces altering frequencies in the idealized model. The conditional equation is useful precisely because deviations force us to seek which condition is unmet.

Biology is no less scientific for giving conditions importance. The problem would be presenting conditions as optional details. No prediction about a trait’s success is serious if it forgets the environment in which success is measured.

There is another complication: organisms modify the environment selecting them. A human community can change its institutions, resource access and support for children or vulnerable people. Without attributing precise genetic mechanisms to particular social changes, we can observe the logical relation: if environment matters for advantage, changing the environment can change the advantage. ‘Natural’ does not mean ‘independent of what we do’.

Darwin also discusses social instincts, sympathy and sexual selection. His writings nevertheless contain judgments marked by his era’s hierarchies and prejudices. Reading them as foundational texts does not require turning every passage into contemporary authority. The principle of selection must be separated from speculative historical applications and moral hierarchies attributed to human groups (Darwin, 1871/1874) .

When someone invokes ‘the laws of biology’ to declare that social assistance contradicts nature, the answer need not be denying evolution. We ask which model, variable and evidence support the claim. Support, cooperation and institutions are also processes in the natural world. The existence of selection does not entail that we ought to let someone suffer, just as the existence of infections does not entail that we ought to avoid treatment.

Who benefits biologically from the ability to identify regularities? In an environment where anticipation changes opportunities for action, a system learning useful relationships may have an advantage. But ‘useful’ and ‘completely true’ are not identical. A simplified rule can guide local action well and mislead in another domain. This is a possibility argument, not proof that every human error is a selected adaptation.

This is precisely where improvised evolutionary stories must be avoided. We can quickly invent a story about the advantage of a belief, generosity or cruelty. Empirical support requires comparisons, mechanisms, measurements and alternatives. That an explanation seems plausible retrospectively does not prove the process happened that way.

Nor do economic and biological success overlap by definition. Income, status, number of children, survival of descendants and well-being are different variables. Saying a group ‘wins’ without specifying the indicator may conceal a change of subject. Having more descendants does not demonstrate intellectual or moral superiority; having more money does not demonstrate a hereditary advantage.

Life ultimately teaches us to conceive laws without erasing history. General regularity and contingent event are not adversaries. A rule can explain why certain differences matter, while history can explain why precisely those differences were available. Between them appears a world where success is real, contextual and in no way a cosmic verdict on a being’s worth.
